n: Chapter 9 contrasts two hostesses inviting guests to two feasts. Wisdom has built a sturdy, beautiful house with seven pillars—seven suggesting completeness and perfection.

f.g: Seven often symbolizes completeness; a grand, well-built house.

n: She has prepared a rich banquet: meat slaughtered, wine mixed with spices, and the table set.

f.g: Mixed wine, often with spices or water, for a feast.

n: She sends out her servant girls and calls from the highest points of the city.

f.w: upon the highest places of the city

n: Her invitation is to the naive and those lacking sense—exactly those who need her most.
Come eat my bread and drink my wine. Christians may hear an echo of Christ’s invitation to the bread of life and the sacrament.
Leave foolishness behind and live; walk in the way of understanding.
A brief interlude on teaching: correcting a mocker only brings you insult and abuse.

f.g: A stain or injury—abuse thrown back at you.

n: Don’t waste correction on scoffers—they’ll hate you. But correct a wise person and they will love you for it. How we respond to correction reveals our character.

f.w: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee

n: Teach the wise and righteous and they will grow even wiser. Learning builds on learning.
The theme of the whole book returns: reverence for the Lord is where wisdom starts, and knowing the Holy One is true understanding.

f.w: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom

f.g: Hebrew plural, often understood as “the Holy One”—God himself.

n: Wisdom speaks again: through her your days will be lengthened.
Each person reaps their own choices. Wisdom benefits you; scoffing hurts you alone. This stresses personal responsibility.
Now the second hostess: Folly, pictured as a loud, ignorant woman.
She sits in her doorway on a seat in the city’s high places—copying Wisdom’s location to compete with her.

f.w: a seat in the high places of the city

n: She calls to passers-by who are minding their own business, trying to pull them off their straight path.

f.g: passengers = passers-by, travelers on the road.

n: Her invitation uses the exact words of Wisdom’s (verse 4). Temptation often imitates the good to deceive.

f.w: Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither

n: Folly’s menu: stolen water and secret bread—the thrill of the forbidden. Her feast offers only what is stolen, while Wisdom offers a real banquet.

f.g: Often understood as a metaphor for illicit sexual pleasure.

n: The guest doesn’t realize her house is full of the dead—her past guests are in the depths of the grave. The two invitations lead to life or to death.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol—the grave, realm of the dead.
